compliboard.text:
Yes, you need a stormwater permit. 
Because you have industrial activity exposed to stormwater, you must obtain coverage under Oregon's 1200-Z permit
. 
A "no exposure" certification—which would exempt you from the permit—requires all industrial materials and activities be protected by storm-resistant shelter to prevent exposure to precipitation
. Your drums are not covered, so that exemption does not apply.


The current 1200-Z permit took effect July 1, 2026
. You apply through Oregon DEQ's Your DEQ Online system; 
fees are listed in Table 70G, and activity fees may also apply
. 
The permit requires you to develop a stormwater pollution control plan and comply with monitoring and sampling requirements
.

For spill containment: 
Federal EPA rules require secondary containment capacity equal to the larger of 100% of your largest single drum or 10% of the total volume of all drums
. 
The system must also hold at least 10% of total volume or 100% of the largest container, whichever is larger
, and 
must either prevent precipitation from entering or have capacity to accommodate rainwater
. 
States can enforce stricter requirements than the federal minimum
.


Oregon Fire Code requires spill control for storage of hazardous material liquids where individual vessels exceed 55 gallons or aggregate capacity exceeds 1,000 gallons
. Depending on how many drums you store, Oregon may require containment beyond the federal baseline.

The 1200-Z permit itself will require you to address spill prevention and containment in your stormwater pollution control plan. Moving your solvents indoors or under cover would eliminate the stormwater permit requirement entirely, but outdoor storage requires both the permit and physical containment.

Confirm the specific containment capacity requirement with Oregon DEQ or the Oregon Fire Marshal—what you need depends on total drum count and whether state rules impose a higher standard than the federal 10%-or-largest-drum rule.

chatgpt.text:
Yes—potentially, and the uncovered solvent-drum pad is a signiﬁcant factor. The answer turns
on your facility’s industrial activity/SIC code, where the stormwater goes, and whether the
solvents are exposed to precipitation.
1. Stormwater permit
Oregon DEQ’s current 1200-Z Industrial Stormwater General Permit took effect July 1,
2026. It regulates stormwater discharges from covered industrial activities to waters of the state.
Importantly, having solvent drums outdoors does not by itself automatically mean you need
a 1200-Z permit. The facility has to fall within one of the industrial categories covered by the
permit. If it does, outdoor storage/handling of solvents can make the activity subject to
stormwater requirements.
For example, DEQ's sector requirements can speciﬁcally address containerized materials such as
solvents and require them to be protected from stormwater exposure.
There is another wrinkle for Hillsboro: if the pad drains to an underground injection control
(UIC) system/drywell, Oregon has separate requirements for industrial/commercial facilities
handling hazardous substances. DEQ requires those facilities to prevent stormwater from being
exposed to hazardous substances before it enters the UIC system.
2. Spill containment
If your facility is subject to the 1200-Z permit, secondary containment is generally the
expectation for hazardous substances/chemical liquids exposed to stormwater. DEQ's
stormwater requirements call for hazardous substances and chemical liquids with potential to
contaminate stormwater to be stored within berms or other secondary containment; where that
isn't practicable, they must be kept in areas that don't drain off-site or to the storm sewer.
So, for an uncovered pad holding solvent drums, I would not treat an ordinary paved pad with
a storm drain as adequate spill containment. A typical compliant approach would be something
like:
•impervious pad;
•curbing/berm or a containment pallet/system;
•enough capacity for the applicable spill plus rainfall/freeboard;
•no uncontrolled connection to a storm drain;
controlled removal of accumulated rainwater;
•inspection for leaks and deterioration;
•spill-response materials and procedures; and
•protection against vehicle impacts and drum damage.
DEQ's industrial stormwater guidance speciﬁcally recommends keeping drums/containers
containing signiﬁcant materials or hazardous substances away from drainage pathways and
surface waters.
3. There may also be ﬁre-code requirements
If these are ﬂammable solvents, Oregon OSHA's ﬂammable-liquid rules can independently
require the storage area to be graded to divert spills or surrounded by a curb, with drainage
arranged so spills don't create a hazard.
Oregon's State Fire Marshal also regulates/reporting certain quantities of hazardous substances
under the Community Right to Know program.
What I would need to give you a fairly deﬁnitive answer
If you give me these four facts, I can work through the Oregon requirements for your speciﬁc
Hillsboro site:
1.What does the facility manufacture/process? (or your SIC code, if you know it)
2.Are these virgin solvent drums, used/spent solvent, or both?
3.Approximately how many gallons are stored on the pad?
4.Where does the pad's rainwater go—storm drain, ditch/creek, UIC/drywell, sanitary
sewer, or does it inﬁltrate on-site?
Those details determine whether you're looking at 1200-Z coverage, UIC requirements,
hazardous-waste requirements, ﬁre-code containment, or several of them simultaneously.

gemini.text:
Stormwater Permit Requirements in Hillsboro, Oregon
If you store drums of solvent outdoors on an uncovered pad exposed to rain, yes, you
will very likely need an industrial stormwater permit.
!The Oregon DEQ 1200-Z Permit: The Oregon Department of Environmental
Quality (DEQ) regulates stormwater runoff from industrial sites under the 1200-Z
General NPDES Permit.
!No "No Exposure" Exclusion: Because your solvent drums are outdoors and
exposed to precipitation, your site does not qualify for a "No Exposure" exclusion. If
stormwater from your facility ﬂows off the pad and into surface waters, ditches, or
municipal storm sewer systems (managed locally in Hillsboro via Clean Water
Services infrastructure), permit coverage is mandatory.
!High Pollution Risk: Uncovered solvent storage is a major red ﬂag for stormwater
inspections. Rainwater washing over the pad can pick up chemical residue or minor
drips, creating a high risk of benchmark exceedances and heavy penalties.
Spill Containment and Secondary Containment Rules
Storing hazardous liquids like solvents outdoors on an unroofed pad also triggers strict
secondary containment requirements under federal and state environmental laws.
!Volume Sizing: Your secondary containment system must be capable of holding
the greater of 110% of the volume of your largest drum or 10% of the total
aggregate volume of all containers on the pad.
!The Rainwater Problem: Because your pad is uncovered, your containment
structure will ﬁll up with rainwater.
!You must design the containment to hold both the required spill volume plus the
heavy runoff volume generated by a major design storm (such as a 24-hour, 25-
year storm event), or use physical berms to prevent outside run-on.
!Water Disposal: Accumulated rainwater inside a solvent containment basin is
considered potentially contaminated industrial wastewater. You cannot drain it
into a storm sewer. It must be tested, managed, and hauled off-site for proper
disposal unless explicitly permitted otherwise.
Recommended Best Practices
To drastically reduce your compliance burden, lower your risk of spills, and avoid
expensive wastewater management fees, consider these solutions:
!Build a Roof or Canopy: Installing a structural roof or heavy-duty cover over the
pad—along with perimeter curbing to block stormwater run-on—prevents rain from
ever touching the drums.
!Relocate Indoors: Moving your solvent inventory inside a warehouse or a
dedicated chemical storage locker is the safest and most compliant option.
!Coordinate Locally: Contact Clean Water Services (CWS) (the water resource
management district for Washington County/Hillsboro) or an environmental
consultant to verify your speciﬁc SIC code requirements and site drainage setup.
Would you like help outlining a Stormwater Pollution Control Plan (SWPCP) for your
facility?

claude.text:
Short answer: yes to both, almost certainly, given what you've described.
Stormwater — 1200-Z permit
Oregon regulates this through DEQ's 1200-Z Industrial Stormwater Discharge General Permit,
and the trigger isn't complicated: if your industrial activity area is exposed to precipitation and
that stormwater discharges — even indirectly through a ditch, storm drain, or sheet ﬂow — to a
water of the state, you need coverage. The classic example DEQ itself uses is materials stored
outside where rain falls on the storage area and washes into the stormwater system — that's
exactly your drum pad. City of Estacada
The one escape hatch is a "No Exposure Certiﬁcation" — but that only applies when industrial
materials and activities are not exposed to stormwater (i.e., everything's under a roof or
otherwise shielded). Since you're describing an uncovered pad with drums sitting directly in the
rain, that exemption isn't available to you. You're in coverage-required territory, not exemption
territory.
Whether solvent storage/distribution speciﬁcally falls under a covered sector depends on your
SIC code and activity classiﬁcation under the permit's Table 1/2 — coverage applies when
stormwater is associated with an industrial activity identiﬁed in those tables, or when DEQ
notiﬁes a facility it needs coverage. Chemical storage and distribution operations are typically
captured. Practically, the move is to register in Your DEQ Online, get your site's Standard
Industrial Classiﬁcation conﬁrmed, and if covered, develop a Stormwater Pollution Control Plan
(SWPCP) — that's the document where the pad, the drums, and your containment measures all
get described and where DEQ will look ﬁrst if there's ever a spill or an inspection. Oregon
Department of Environmental Quality
One more thing worth ﬂagging: DEQ just reissued 1200-Z effective July 1, 2026, replacing the
2021 version, so if anyone on your team was working off old guidance, get the current permit
text rather than an older PDF.
Spill containment for the same pad
This is a separate obligation from the stormwater permit, and it's driven by ﬁre code, not DEQ.
Hillsboro enforces the Oregon Fire Code (based on the International Fire Code), and outdoor
storage of hazardous materials — solvents almost always qualify — requires secondary
containment. The standard the ﬁre marshal will hold you to is containment sized for 110% of the
largest single container, or enough volume to hold the contents of the largest drum plus a safety
margin, with the containment area also needing a way to shed clean rainwater without it
becoming a pathway for spilled product to reach the storm drain (usually a manually-operated
valve or absorbent-sock drain, not a passive open drain).
Two more layers to check:
If any of what's in those drums is petroleum-based and your aggregate aboveground storage
exceeds 1,320 gallons, you're also into SPCC (Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure)
territory under EPA's 40 CFR 112 — that requires a written SPCC plan, not just physical
containment.
And if any of the material is hazardous waste rather than virgin product, RCRA secondary
containment rules (40 CFR 264/265 Subpart I) kick in with their own specs on containment
system design, including things like a minimum containment capacity and compatibility of the
containment liner with what's stored.
Practical sequencing: get the pad physically compliant ﬁrst (curbing or berm sized to the 110%
rule, with a controlled drain), because that containment design is also exactly what you'll
describe in the SWPCP for the stormwater permit — the two requirements reinforce each other
rather than being independent paperwork exercises. I'd loop in Hillsboro Fire & Rescue's hazmat
inspector directly since local ﬁre code enforcement varies by jurisdiction in exact numbers and
drain valve requirements, and DEQ's regional NW ofﬁce for the 1200-Z application speciﬁcs.

compliboard_templated.text:
# STORMWATER PERMIT & SPILL CONTAINMENT FOR OUTDOOR SOLVENT STORAGE IN HILLSBORO, OREGON

## WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

**Yes, you almost certainly need a stormwater permit.** In Oregon, industrial facilities that have stormwater runoff exposed to industrial materials must obtain coverage under the **1200-Z General Permit** (Industrial Stormwater). Storing drums of solvent outdoors where rain can contact them, or where spills could be washed away by rain, is exactly the kind of activity this permit regulates.

**And yes, you need spill containment.** Oregon's rules require secondary containment for outdoor chemical storage. This means you can't just keep drums sitting on an open pad — you need something to catch spills and leaks before they reach stormwater drains or the ground.

## WHO IT APPLIES TO

- **Any industrial facility in Oregon** with outdoor activities or materials exposed to stormwater
- **Specifically applies to you** because solvents are industrial materials, and you're storing them uncovered where rain hits them
- The permit requirement isn't based on company size or number of drums — if you're doing this activity, you need the permit
- Hillsboro is in the Portland metro area, so you're also in the **DEQ's Northwest Region** jurisdiction

## THE KEY FACTS

### Stormwater Permit (1200-Z)

- Issued by the **Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ)**
- Requires you to submit a **Notice of Intent (NOI)** before you can legally operate
- You must develop a **Stormwater Pollution Control Plan (SWPCP)** that identifies:
  - Where stormwater contacts industrial materials
  - What pollutants could get into runoff
  - What controls you'll use to prevent contamination
  - How you'll inspect and maintain those controls
- You must conduct **visual monitoring** of your stormwater discharge regularly
- **Annual reporting** is required
- Permit fee: approximately $565/year (subject to change)

### Spill Containment Requirements

- Oregon requires **secondary containment** for hazardous substance storage
- For drums on a pad, this typically means:
  - A **spill pallet or berm** that holds at least 110% of the largest container's volume
  - Or a **concrete containment pad** with curbs/walls and a drain valve
  - The containment must be **impervious** (won't leak into soil)
- Any captured stormwater in your containment must be:
  - **Inspected** before release
  - **Treated as hazardous waste** if contaminated
  - Possibly tested, depending on the solvent type

### What You Need to Do Right Now

1. **Stop storing drums uncovered immediately** — get temporary containment in place (tarps are a short-term fix only)
2. **File for your 1200-Z permit** — submit an NOI to DEQ
3. **Install proper secondary containment** — spill pallets or a bermed pad
4. **Create your SWPCP** — this is your operating manual for stormwater management
5. **Train your employees** on spill response and stormwater protection

## COMMON MISCONCEPTIONS

**"We only have a few drums, so we don't need a permit."**  
Wrong. There's no minimum threshold based on quantity. If you're an industrial facility with outdoor exposure, you need the permit.

**"We'll just cover the drums with a tarp."**  
Not good enough for compliance. You still need secondary containment beneath them in case of leaks or spills. A tarp also doesn't qualify as proper coverage under the permit — you'd need a permanent roof or enclosed structure.

**"Rainwater that falls on the pad is clean until a spill happens."**  
No. Even small drips, residue on drum lids, or vapors can contaminate stormwater. DEQ assumes any rain contacting your storage area is potentially polluted.

**"We're too small for DEQ to care."**  
Size doesn't matter. DEQ enforces these rules on small businesses regularly. Complaints from neighbors or downstream water sampling can trigger inspections.

**"Spill containment is just an OSHA thing."**  
It's both. OSHA cares about worker safety; DEQ cares about environmental contamination. You need containment to satisfy both agencies.

## WHAT HAPPENS IF YOU IGNORE IT

### Stormwater Permit Violations

- **Civil penalties**: Up to $25,000 per day per violation under Oregon law
- **Federal fines**: EPA can also enforce, with penalties up to $59,973 per day (yes, per day)
- **Stop-work orders**: DEQ can shut down your outdoor operations until you're compliant
- **Mandatory corrective action**: You'll be ordered to fix the problem at your expense, often on a tight timeline

### Lack of Spill Containment

- **Immediate cleanup orders**: If a spill reaches soil or water, you pay for environmental remediation (often tens of thousands of dollars)
- **Hazardous waste liability**: You're responsible for contaminated soil removal and disposal
- **Third-party lawsuits**: If your runoff contaminates a neighbor's property or waterway, you can be sued
- **Criminal charges**: Knowing violations that endanger public health can result in criminal prosecution

### Real-World Consequences

Oregon DEQ actively patrols industrial areas and responds to complaints. In the Portland metro area (which includes Hillsboro), enforcement is particularly active. A single rainfall event that washes solvent residue into a storm drain can trigger a violation notice within days.

## USEFUL RESOURCES

### Oregon DEQ

- **1200-Z General Permit information**: https://www.oregon.gov/deq/wq/wqpermits/Pages/NPDES-Stormwater-1200Z.aspx
- **DEQ Northwest Region Office** (serves Hillsboro):  
  700 NE Multnomah St., Suite 600, Portland, OR 97232  
  Phone: (503) 229-5696
- **File your Notice of Intent (NOI)**: Available on the DEQ website above

### Spill Containment Guidance

- **DEQ Hazardous Waste Program**: https://www.oregon.gov/deq/hazardouswaste  
  Phone: (503) 229-5913
- **EPA Secondary Containment Guidance**: Useful technical details on sizing and design

### Where to Buy Compliance Equipment

- Look for **spill pallets** rated for your solvent type (check chemical compatibility)
- Many industrial supply companies in the Portland area sell compliant containment systems
- Budget approximately $100-$500 per pallet depending on capacity

### Consultant Help

If this feels overwhelming, consider hiring an environmental consultant who specializes in Oregon stormwater permits. They can:
- Prepare your NOI and SWPCP
- Design your containment system
- Train your staff
- Typical cost: $2,000-$5,000 for initial setup

---

**Bottom line:** Get compliant now. File for the permit, install containment, and document everything. The cost of compliance is far less than the cost of a violation, and Oregon DEQ does not look kindly on businesses that pollute stormwater with industrial chemicals.

verdict.ranking: Claude 1st · ChatGPT and Gemini close behind with OPPOSITE failure modes · CompliBoard last, clearly.
verdict.compliboard_is_weakest: CONFIRMED. It is the only one to overstate the trigger, the only one to omit BOTH the exemption and the reissue, the only one with unsourced figures, the only one that asked nothing — and the only one that knew who was asking. It is also the longest, at 1010 words against 420-611.
verdict.claude_is_strongest: CONFIRMED. Only answer to pass the way-out, currency and sourcing criteria together, and the only one to cite regulations by number or to say what to do about the reissue.
verdict.where_this_scoring_DISAGREES_with_the_ow: The owner read it as 'Claude and ChatGPT strongest'. On the criterion the owner himself called decisive — the No Exposure Certification, the route by which no permit is needed — CHATGPT MISSES IT AND GEMINI CATCHES IT. ChatGPT names the sector gate, which is a different mechanism. So ChatGPT and Gemini are not cleanly ordered: ChatGPT is better on currency, on stating the trigger, and on asking the right questions; Gemini is better on the single thing that decides whether the answer applies at all. Ranking ChatGPT above Gemini overall is defensible; calling it joint-strongest understates what Gemini caught.
verdict.what_it_does_not_settle: Three of the four were single runs of a bare model with no context. A different run could name the exemption or drop the date. The benchmark is repeatable for that reason.
